history.title:
381
Founded
history.text: In the 11th year of King Sosurim of Goguryeo, the monk Ado established Jin Jong-sa here, marking the beginning of Jeondeungsa's long history. Over the Three Kingdoms period, this temple grew into an important Buddhist center.

history.title:
1282
Renamed to Jeondeungsa
history.text: With Queen Jeonghwa's sponsorship, the Chinese Lotus Sutra was enshrined here, and the temple's name was changed to 'Jeondeungsa'. From this time, the temple became a significant place for both doctrinal study and practice in state Buddhism.

history.title:
1621
Major Reconstruction
history.text: After fires in 1605 and 1614, large-scale reconstruction began in 1615 and was completed with Monk Jigyeong's ridgepole ceremony in 1621. The present core temple layout dates largely from this period.

history.title:
1726
Royal Connection
history.text: King Yeongjo personally bestowed the plaque 'Chwihyangdang (Hall of Drunken Fragrance)', elevating Jeondeungsa's status. This royal attention shows that Jeondeungsa was more than a local temple; it held national significance.

history.title:
18th Century
National Role
history.text: At Jeondeungsa, the royal archives (Sago) and granary (Jeongjokchang) were established to safeguard royal records and provisions. This reveals the temple's role in state affairs beyond its religious function.

history.title:
1911
Modern Jeondeungsa
history.text: After the Temple Ordinance of 1911, Jeondeungsa was designated as a head temple overseeing 34 monasteries in Ganghwa, Gaeseong, Gimpo, and beyond. Throughout the 20th century, major halls such as the Main Buddha Hall, Underworld Hall, Daedjoru, and Samseonggak were rebuilt, refining the temple complex.

history.title:
Today
Tradition and the Present
history.text: Jeondeungsa preserves numerous cultural assets, including treasure-class halls, woodblocks, and Buddhist statues. At the same time, through the Samnangseong History and Culture Festival, templestay programs, and cultural experiences, it continues to connect tradition with contemporary life as a living temple.

heritage.title: Daeungbojeon Hall
heritage.description:
Treasure No. 178
Daeungbojeon Hall, built in 1621, is a wooden building with a 3-bay front and side. It is considered a masterpiece of mid-Joseon architecture due to its neat structure and exquisite carving decorations.

heritage.title: Yaksajeon Hall
heritage.description:
Treasure No. 179
Yaksajeon Hall, located west of Daeungbojeon Hall, is a 3-bay paljak-jiibung building of the mid-Joseon period with a multi-bracket system. Its structure and decoration are similar to those of Daeungbojeon Hall.

heritage.title: Jeondeungsa Iron Bell
heritage.description:
Treasure No. 393
A uniquely shaped bell produced in Songmyeongsa, China in 1097. It was taken by the Japanese during the colonial period and returned to Jeondeungsa after liberation.

heritage.title: Wooden Seokgiyorae Sambul Jwasang (Three Buddhas Statue)
heritage.description: This is a statue of three Buddhas (Samsebul) created in 1623 with Suyeon participating as the chief monk. The main Buddha, Sakyamuni Buddha, shows stable proportions and refined sculptural beauty.

heritage.title: Wooden Jijangbosal Samjon Sang and Siwang Sang Ilgwal (Bodhisattva of Earth Store Triad and Ten Kings of Hell)
heritage.description: The statue of Jijangbosal and 31 attendants in Jeondeungsa Myeongbujeon Hall were created in 1636. The Jijang Samjon Sang and Siwang Sang have unique and beautiful sculptural aesthetics and are well preserved.

heritage.title: Myobeopyeonhwagyeong Woodblocks
heritage.description: These are 104 plates and 411 sheets of the Lotus Sutra, a Mahayana scripture, re-engraved at Jeongsu Temple in 1543. The preservation is good, but there is some damage, and one plate was lost during the Korean War.

heritage.title: Myeonggyeongdae (Mirror Stand)
heritage.description: A pair of Buddhist wooden crafts made in 1627, depicting blue and yellow lions supporting a mirror with flame patterns. It symbolizes the mirror that reflects sins in hell and is considered important material for studying Buddhist wooden crafts of the late Joseon Dynasty.
